Q1: Supervised learning fits a function from labeled pairs (x, y), so the target output is known for every training example. Grouping unlabeled points is clustering, an unsupervised task.
Q2: By convention each row of the data matrix is one observation and each column is one feature, so an n by d matrix holds n data points with d features each. It is rarely square.
Q3: A convolution replaces each pixel by a weighted sum of its neighbourhood, which is a linear filter; the weights decide whether it smooths (averaging) or extracts features such as edges.
Q4: Reinforcement learning is defined by an agent choosing actions in states and receiving rewards, learning a policy from that feedback. Supervised learning has fixed labels, not rewards.
Q5: Linear regression is fitted by least squares, which minimizes the sum of squared errors, so its loss is the quadratic loss. Logistic regression uses the logistic loss and SVMs the hinge loss.
Q6: An SVM picks the separating hyperplane with the largest margin to the closest training points, the support vectors. Minimizing the count of errors alone gives no unique boundary and generalizes worse.
Q7: The hinge loss is zero once a point is on the correct side with margin at least 1 and grows linearly otherwise, which is exactly the SVM margin objective. Logistic regression uses the logistic loss.
Q8: A false negative is an actual positive that the model predicted as negative. A false positive is the reverse: an actual negative predicted as positive.
Q9: The F-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR/(P+R) for F1, so it is low unless both are high. Accuracy ignores the precision and recall split, and AUC is threshold-free.
Q10: The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the classification threshold moves. Precision against recall is a different curve.
Q11: The sigmoid squashes the linear score w'x into (0, 1) so it can be read as P(y=1|x). It does not make the model non-linear: the decision boundary is still the hyperplane w'x = 0.
Q12: Regularization adds a penalty on large weights, which restricts model flexibility and so counters overfitting. It makes underfitting more likely, not less.
Q13: PCA finds orthogonal directions ordered by the variance they capture and projects the data onto the first few, minimizing projection error. It uses no class labels; maximizing class separation is LDA.
Q14: A kernel returns the inner product of two points in a high-dimensional feature space without ever constructing that space, so a linear method there becomes a non-linear classifier in the input space.
Q15: k-NN stores the training instances and classifies a new point by the majority class among its k nearest stored examples, so it is instance-based (memory-based) learning with no parametric model.
Q16: The split is chosen to maximize information gain (the entropy reduction) or equivalently to minimize Gini impurity in the child nodes. Maximum margin is an SVM principle, not a tree criterion.
Q17: Random forests add to bagging a random subset of features at each candidate split, which reduces the influence of strong features and decorrelates the trees. Both build trees independently, not sequentially.
Q18: The Parzen estimator takes the region R small enough that the density is roughly constant inside it, so the mass P is about P(x) times the volume V. Growing V until it holds k points is the k-NN estimator.
Q19: Feature engineering means hand-crafting new input features from raw data using domain knowledge, such as zero-crossing rate for voice detection. Feature selection only picks a subset of existing features.
Q20: Bagging averages (or votes over) many models trained on bootstrap samples, which cancels much of their random variation; it reduces variance without affecting bias.
Q21: K-means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares: the total squared distance from each point to the centroid of its assigned cluster. Each iteration lowers it by reassigning points and recomputing centroids.
Q22: DBSCAN grows clusters through density-connected core points, so it follows any shape and leaves low-density points labeled as noise. K-means assumes compact, roughly spherical clusters and assigns every point.
Q23: MLE picks the parameter values under which the observed data have the highest probability (likelihood). Priors are not involved; they enter only in Bayesian or MAP estimation.
Q24: Bayes' rule multiplies the likelihood P(D|theta) by the prior P(theta) to get the posterior P(theta|D) up to a normalizing constant. The MLE is a point estimate, not an input to this rule.
Q25: Aleatoric uncertainty is the noise built into the data-generating process itself, so more data cannot remove it. Epistemic uncertainty comes from limited data or knowledge and does shrink with more data.
Q26: The binomial counts successes in a fixed number N of independent trials with the same success probability. The number of trials until the first success is the geometric distribution.
Q27: Clustering uses no labels: it finds structure in the inputs alone, which is unsupervised learning. Semi-supervised learning mixes a few labeled points with many unlabeled ones.
Q28: Maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood in mu gives the sample mean, since the derivative of the sum of squared deviations vanishes there. The median is the MLE for a Laplace distribution, not a Gaussian.
Q29: The agent must trade off exploring actions whose value is uncertain against exploiting the action that currently looks best; too little exploration locks in a poor arm, too much wastes reward.
Q30: A contextual bandit observes a feature vector (context) before each choice and conditions its action on it, while the plain multi-armed bandit has a single fixed state. Neither one has delayed rewards.
Q31: The UCB bonus grows with sqrt(ln t / N_a), so it is largest for arms pulled few times, whose value estimate is still uncertain. Arms pulled often get a small bonus because their estimate is reliable.
Q32: Backpropagation applies the chain rule layer by layer to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. The forward pass computes the outputs; the gradient step itself is the optimizer's job.
Q33: Convolutional layers slide learned filters over the input, and stacking them builds features from edges up to object parts. Pooling only down-samples and fully connected layers discard the spatial layout.
Q34: An RNN carries a hidden state from one step to the next, applying the same learned function each time, so earlier inputs influence later outputs. Parallel processing with no memory describes a transformer.
Q35: In a plain RNN the gradient is multiplied through every time step, so it vanishes or explodes over long gaps and distant dependencies cannot be learned. LSTM gates let information pass through many steps unchanged.
Q36: Pooling summarizes each small window by one value, shrinking the feature map and making the output tolerant of small shifts. It has no learned parameters and adds no non-linearity.
Q37: Word2Vec trains a shallow network to predict context words from a target word (skip-gram) or the target from its context (CBOW); the learned weights are the embeddings. Bag-of-words and TF-IDF only count words.
Q38: Attention scores every position by query-key similarity and forms a weighted sum of their values, so the model focuses on the relevant parts of the sequence. A GRU is a recurrent gate, not attention.
Q39: An LLM is trained on huge text corpora to predict the next token given the preceding ones, and its other abilities emerge from that objective. Retrieval and image classification are separate tasks.
Q40: NLP is the processing of human language, as text or speech, by computers. Images, sensor streams and numeric tables are handled by other branches of machine learning.
Q41: The L2 penalty on the squared weights shrinks every weight toward zero in proportion to its size, so weights get small but stay non-zero. Setting weights exactly to zero is what the L1 (lasso) penalty does.
Q42: A degree-10 polynomial has enough freedom to follow the noise in a small dataset, so training error drops while test error rises: high variance, overfitting. Underfitting comes from a degree that is too low.
Q43: Logistic regression outputs probabilities, and the logistic loss is the negative log-likelihood of the labels under those probabilities, so minimizing it is maximum likelihood. SVMs use the hinge loss.
Q44: Precision is TP/(TP+FP): of all samples predicted positive, the fraction that truly are positive. The fraction of actual positives that were found is recall, TP/(TP+FN).
Q45: The ROC curve is traced by sweeping the threshold from 0 to 1, so the area under it summarizes ranking quality over all thresholds at once. Accuracy and F-score depend on one chosen threshold.
Q46: High bias with low variance means the model is too simple to capture the true relationship and errs the same way on every dataset: underfitting. Overfitting is the opposite, low bias and high variance.
Q47: Recall is TP/(TP+FN), so higher recall means fewer missed positives, which matters when a missed diagnosis is costly. Higher precision only reduces false alarms, and equal accuracy says nothing about this split.
Q48: Slack variables measure how far each point violates the margin, and the objective adds C times their sum to the margin term, trading margin width against violations. Lagrange multipliers arise only in the dual form.
Q49: In high dimensions the training points become sparse and all distances grow similar, so the nearest neighbours stop being meaningfully close: the curse of dimensionality. Vanishing gradients belong to deep networks.
Q50: Greedy means each split is chosen to maximize the impurity decrease at that node alone, with no look-ahead at how later splits turn out. Optimizing the whole tree at once would be exponentially expensive.
Q51: Pruning cuts back branches of a fully grown tree whose estimated error is no better than their parent's, removing structure that only fitted noise. Bagging and boosting build ensembles instead.
Q52: For classification the bagged trees each vote for a class and the majority wins (averaging predicted probabilities is the alternative). Sequential error correction is boosting; a trained meta-learner is stacking.
Q53: Extra Trees keep the bagging and random feature subsets of a random forest but also pick each split threshold at random inside the feature's range instead of searching for the best impurity-reducing cut.
Q54: With a very large k the prediction is a vote over much of the dataset, so the boundary becomes smooth and tends toward the majority class: high bias, underfitting. Small k gives the jagged, high-variance boundary.
Q55: Non-parametric methods let the data determine the shape of the function or density instead of fixing a form such as a line or a Gaussian. The price is that they usually need more data and are slower at prediction time.
Q56: The kernel (Parzen window) defines the region R around x: a hypercube or sphere counts points inside, a Gaussian weights them smoothly, and its width sets the size. Fixing a count k is the nearest-neighbour method.
Q57: K-means uses Euclidean distance, so a feature with a large numeric range (income in euros) would dominate one with a small range (height in meters) unless each feature is scaled to a comparable range first.
Q58: A border point lies within epsilon of a core point but has fewer than MinPts neighbours itself, so it joins the cluster without extending it. Noise points are within epsilon of no core point at all.
Q59: The elbow method plots the within-cluster sum of squares against K and picks the K where the curve bends, since adding clusters beyond that point gives little further reduction.
Q60: The principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, which are mutually orthogonal, sorted by eigenvalue so the first captures the most variance. Class separation is LDA, not PCA.
Q61: Adding the same constant vector to all inputs must leave the feature unchanged; the RBF kernel has this property since it depends only on the difference between points. Invariance to scaling is a separate property.
Q62: Hand-crafted features need an expert who knows the domain and take a lot of manual work per problem, while feature learning lets the model derive them from data. Manual features are not more expensive to train on.
Q63: Min-max scaling maps each feature to a fixed range, usually [0, 1], by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the range. Making features Gaussian or removing correlated ones is not what scaling does.
Q64: The kernel gives phi(x_i)'phi(x_j) directly, so phi(x) itself, which may be huge or infinite-dimensional, is never computed. The pairwise inner products are exactly what the kernel does compute.
Q65: The binomial takes only integer values 0 to N, so it is discrete. Gaussian, Student's t and Dirichlet distributions are defined over continuous values and have densities, not probability masses.
Q66: The Gaussian is the continuous distribution fully specified by its mean and variance. Bernoulli and Poisson are discrete, and the uniform is set by its endpoints rather than by mean and variance.
Q67: Bayes' rule gives P(theta|D) = P(D|theta)P(theta)/P(D); the evidence P(D) is a constant in theta, so the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior.
Q68: Putting a distribution over the weights captures how uncertain the model itself is given limited data, which is epistemic uncertainty. Aleatoric noise in the data stays no matter how the weights are modelled.
Q69: The likelihood of independent samples is a product of probabilities, and the log turns it into a sum that is easier to differentiate and avoids numerical underflow; the maximizer is unchanged because log is increasing.
Q70: A Bernoulli trial is a single yes/no outcome with success probability p, and a binomial with N=1 counts successes in exactly one such trial, so the two coincide.
Q71: Independence means knowing B does not change the probability of A, which is equivalent to P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). A zero joint probability instead means A and B are mutually exclusive, a different notion.
Q72: Bayes decision theory computes the posterior P(C_k|x) from class likelihoods and priors and picks the class with the lowest expected risk (highest posterior for 0-1 loss). SVMs and trees output no posterior themselves.
Q73: The activation function maps a neuron's weighted sum to its output and makes it non-linear; without it any stack of layers collapses to one linear map. Weight initialization and learning rates are separate matters.
Q74: Because one filter is reused at every position, a convolutional layer has far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer over the same input. Shared weights give translation equivariance; invariance needs pooling.
Q75: The pooling layer follows convolution and activation and summarizes each small window by one value (its maximum or average), producing a coarser map. Fully connected layers come at the end of the network.
Q76: A GRU merges the forget and input gates into one update gate and drops the separate cell state, keeping only the hidden state, so it has fewer parameters than an LSTM. It still has two gates (update and reset).
Q77: Regret is the cumulative gap between the reward the best arm would have given and the reward actually collected; a low-regret algorithm loses little by exploring. Counting non-optimal pulls ignores how bad they were.
Q78: With probability epsilon the agent ignores its estimates and picks an arm uniformly at random, which is the exploration step; the rest of the time it takes the arm with the highest estimated reward.
Q79: Embeddings are learned so words appearing in similar contexts get nearby vectors, so distances and directions encode meaning and grammatical roles. Word length and raw frequency are not what the vectors represent.
Q80: Self-attention relates every position to every other in one step, with no step-by-step recurrence, so the whole sequence is processed in parallel; this is what makes transformers fast to train on GPUs.
Q81: A hard margin SVM allows no margin violations, so a hyperplane with all points on or outside the margin must exist, which requires linearly separable data. Slack variables belong to the soft margin version.
Q82: The Brier score is the mean squared difference between predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome, and only the true probabilities minimize it, which makes it strictly proper. Accuracy and F-score use hard labels only.
Q83: The L1 penalty on absolute weights has a constant gradient near zero, so the optimum pushes some weights exactly to zero and drops those features. L2 shrinks weights but leaves them non-zero.
Q84: Pre-pruning stops growing a branch early when a node is pure enough, too small, or the tree is at its maximum depth. Post-pruning instead grows the full tree and cuts branches back afterwards.
Q85: A very wide window averages over many distant points, so the estimate becomes very smooth and washes out real structure in the density: high bias. A very narrow window gives the spiky, high-variance estimate.
Q86: 1-NN assigns each location the class of its nearest training point, so the regions are the cells of the Voronoi tessellation and the boundary runs along the cell edges between points of different classes.
Q87: The Gaussian kernel exp(-||x-x'||^2 / 2 sigma^2) is governed by its width: sigma (or gamma = 1/2 sigma^2) sets how fast similarity decays with distance. C is the soft-margin penalty, a separate SVM hyperparameter.
Q88: TF-IDF multiplies the term frequency by the inverse document frequency, so words that occur in few documents get a high weight and common words such as 'the' are down-weighted. Plain TF rewards frequent words.
Q89: Convolution slides a filter across the image, multiplying it element-wise with each patch and summing to give one output pixel; a box filter blurs, a -1/1 filter detects edges. Pooling only picks a maximum or average.
Q90: K-means assigns points to the nearest centroid and updates centroids as means, which minimizes squared Euclidean distance; using another metric changes the objective and the centroid update.
Q91: Each K-means step lowers the within-cluster sum of squares, so it stops at a local minimum that depends on the initial centroids. Different starts can give different results, so the global optimum is not guaranteed.
Q92: A point that is neither a core point nor within epsilon of any core point belongs to no cluster and is labeled noise (an outlier). Border points differ in being reachable from a core point.
Q93: A Bernoulli variable takes value 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1-p, so p is its only parameter; its mean is p and its variance p(1-p). The trial count N belongs to the binomial.
Q94: The expected value is the probability-weighted average of all outcomes, the sum of x times P(x) for a discrete variable. The mode (most likely value) and the median (halfway point) can both differ from it.
Q95: MAP maximizes the posterior, which is likelihood times prior, so the prior pulls the estimate toward values believed plausible; MLE maximizes the likelihood alone. With a flat prior the two coincide.
Q96: Epistemic uncertainty reflects what the model does not know because it has seen too little data, so it is high far from the training points and shrinks with more data. Noise in the process itself is aleatoric.
Q97: Q(s,a) is the expected return, the discounted sum of all future rewards, from taking action a in state s and then following the policy. The immediate reward alone is only its first term.
Q98: The greedy strategy always picks the arm with the highest current estimate and never tries anything else, so it is pure exploitation. Epsilon-greedy, softmax and UCB each add some exploration.
Q99: Dividing by N_a makes the bonus shrink as an arm is pulled more, so arms sampled rarely keep a large bonus and get tried until their estimate is reliable; this is optimism in the face of uncertainty.
Q100: A contextual bandit sees a context (feature vector) before each decision and learns a policy mapping context to action, while a non-contextual bandit only estimates one value per arm. Rewards are immediate in both.
Q101: A neuron computes z = w'x + b and passes it through an activation function f(z), such as a sigmoid or ReLU, to produce its output. Backpropagation and pooling are not part of a single neuron.
Q102: Softmax exponentiates the class scores and normalizes them to sum to 1, giving a probability distribution over all classes. A sigmoid gives one probability per unit and suits binary outputs.
Q103: The learning rate scales each weight update in gradient descent, w <- w - eta * gradient. Backpropagation only computes the gradient; how far to step along it is the optimizer's hyperparameter.
Q104: The stride is the number of pixels the filter moves between successive positions; a stride of 2 halves the output size. Padding and kernel size are set by separate parameters.
Q105: Max pooling keeps only the largest activation in each window, keeping the strongest response and discarding its exact position. Taking the average is average pooling, a different layer.
Q106: ReLU is f(z) = max(0, z): it passes positive inputs unchanged and outputs zero otherwise, which is cheap to compute and keeps the gradient at 1 for positive inputs. Outputs in (0, 1) describe the sigmoid.
Q107: Backpropagation through time multiplies the gradient by the recurrent weight and activation derivative at every step, so over many steps it shrinks exponentially (or explodes). Batch size and softmax are unrelated.
Q108: An LSTM cell uses an input gate, a forget gate and an output gate, each a sigmoid that decides how much to write to, erase from, and read from the cell state. Attention is a transformer component, not an LSTM one.
Q109: Bag-of-words gives each document a vector of word counts over the whole vocabulary: most entries are zero (sparse) and the order of the words is lost. Dense, meaning-bearing vectors come from embeddings.
Q110: A semantic model captures what words and phrases mean and how context changes that meaning, as word embeddings and language models do. Grammatical correctness is the concern of syntactic models.
Q111: Transformers drop the recurrent connections entirely and use self-attention to relate positions, which is why they can process the whole sequence in parallel. Feed-forward layers and softmax outputs remain.
Q112: Each input is projected into a query, a key and a value; attention weights come from the similarity of a query with every key, and the output is the weighted sum of the values.
Q113: Clustering groups data points that are similar to each other without any labels, revealing structure such as customer segments. Predicting prices needs labels, and reward maximization is reinforcement learning.
Q114: The supervised dataset pairs each feature vector x_i with its label or target value y_i; the model parameters w are what gets learned from them, not part of the data.
Q115: Least squares means choosing the weights that minimize the sum of squared residuals, the squared gaps between predicted and actual values. This equals maximum likelihood only under the extra assumption of Gaussian noise.
Q116: Bagging helps when the base models are unstable, so bootstrap resampling produces different models whose errors partly cancel when averaged. Averaging near-identical models changes little.
Q117: A linear kernel is the ordinary inner product, so it fits a linear boundary in the original space; it suits data that are near linearly separable or very high-dimensional, where a linear model already separates well.
Q118: A parametric model fixes the functional form in advance, such as y = w'x + b, so learning only fills in a fixed number of parameters regardless of the data size. Non-parametric models grow with the data.
Q119: Softmax outputs class probabilities, and cross-entropy is the negative log-probability of the true class, so minimizing it is maximum likelihood; with softmax its gradient reduces to prediction minus one-hot target.
Q120: Rewards often arrive long after the actions that caused them, so the learner must work out which earlier decisions deserve the credit or blame; this credit assignment problem is present in every RL setting.
